To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic stress exposure in the borderline hypertensive rat results in the development of hypertension and that the opioid system may play a major role during the maintenance of homeo-stasis in this model.
chronic exposure to a novel, physiological stressor in the BHR is associated with an elevation of arterial blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate.
chronic exposure to a stressor in the borderline hypertensive rat results in an increase in arterial pressure, which is accompanied by an increase in plasma norepinephrine and angiotensin II levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the relationship between stress and arterial hypertension.
elucidating the relationship between stress, hypertension and the central nervous system.
the relationship between stress and development of arterial hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stress and hypertension do have an interactive and interdependent relationship.
stress is a potent stimulus in the development of hypertension, but only in a subset of the population.

chronic stressors are associated with an increase in the incidence and severity of arterial hypertension, and that the central nervous system is involved in the maintenance of this hypertensive state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stress induced hypertensive animal model offers an excellent opportunity to study the interactions between stress and the cardiovascular system.
stress, as a physiological stimulus, is capable of inducing a hypertensive state in the BHR.
the BHR is a useful model for the study of stress induced hypertension and that the endogenous opioids are involved in the regulation of stress induced hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the stress and hypertension relationship is not as simple as previously thought, and that the interaction of stress and the development of hypertension in the BHR is a complex process which involves the central nervous system and the endogenous opioid system.
chronic stress can induce hypertension in BHRs.

chronic exposure to a mild physiological stressor, in the presence of a genetically predisposed hypertensive state, can lead to the development of hypertension and the activation of the endogenous enkephalinergic system.
